# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Purpose

This directory is a workspace for developing and iterating on global Claude Code skills. Skills are installed at `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and are available across all projects.

## Installed skills

The canonical "when to reach for each" catalog is `skills/pathfinder/SKILL.md` (`/pathfinder`); this table is the short index. The external `tab-setup` skill is excluded here — see Boot hooks and Syncing below.

## Review agents (subagent panel)

Domain-expert reviewer personas live in `agents/<name>.md` and deploy to `~/.claude/agents/` via `sync.sh push`. They are **invokable subagent types** (spawned with the `Agent` tool / `subagent_type`), not slash-command skills. Each is **review-only** — it reports findings (severity-tagged, with a summary table) and never rewrites the target. They are designed to run **individually or as a parallel panel** (spawn several in one message for a multi-reviewer read).

<!-- gen-docs:agents:start (generated by scripts/gen-docs.sh from agents/*.md catalog frontmatter — do not hand-edit) -->
| Agent | Domain | Reviews for |
|---|---|---|
| `attribution-reviewer` | Climate attribution | Counterfactual, baseline, framing, uncertainty, model adequacy, overclaiming (PR/OR/ChIP, storyline, D&A) |
| `stats-reviewer` | Statistics / ML | Estimator properties, causal ID, inference under dependence, specification, multiple testing, calibration |
| `meteo-reviewer` | Meteorology (AMS CCM) | Dynamical/thermodynamic consistency, physical basis, observational adequacy, competing drivers, hydrology |
| `scicomm-reviewer` | Science communication | Message Box, narrative, stakes/framing, audience, quantification (full COMPASS portfolio) |
<!-- gen-docs:agents:end -->

All four share `tools: Read, Grep, Glob` and `model: opus`.

### Agent file format & gotcha

Same YAML frontmatter as skills (`name`, `description`, `tools`, `model`). **Critical:** the loader silently drops any agent whose frontmatter fails to parse — the `.md` deploys fine but the type never registers, and it only surfaces in a *fresh* session (the type list is snapshotted at session start). The classic failure is an **unquoted multi-line `description` containing `": "` (colon-space)** on a wrapped line, which YAML reads as a stray mapping key. **Always single-quote multi-line descriptions** (`description: '...'`). `sync.sh push` runs `lint_frontmatter()` to strict-parse every agent's *and* skill's frontmatter (and check the description cap) before deploying, and `.github/workflows/lint.yml` enforces the same in CI. It also runs `lint_skill_refs()`, which checks that every backticked `` `/slash-command` `` resolves to a real skill in `skills/` (or an allowlisted Claude Code built-in) — so a launcher like `grill-me` (whose body is just "Run a `/grilling` session.") can't silently no-op if its target is renamed or deleted. It scans skill bodies and their companion `.md` files at any depth, agent files, and the prose docs (`CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, `docs/**.md`) — renames routinely land in `skills/` but not in the prose. Three allowlists, in descending order of preference: `SCOPED_REFS` for `(file, command)` pairs where one file has a reason to name a non-skill command (the `/resume` explanations); `BUILTINS` for genuine Claude Code built-ins, legitimate anywhere; `PLACEHOLDERS` for prose stand-ins like `` `/slash` `` that aren't commands at all. Prefer `SCOPED_REFS` — a repo-wide entry disables detection in every other file. A third lint, `lint_templates()`, runs `tests/smoke_repo_init.py` on every push/lint (and in CI): templates a skill stamps into *other* repos (repo-init's `TEMPLATES.md`) are invisible to the frontmatter/ref lints, so the smoke test parses every fenced toml/yaml/python block, materializes the gitignores in an isolated tmp repo to assert the tracked/ignored contract, and spot-checks known-wrong-but-parseable values (pre-commit hook ids). Two shipped-class bugs (a git-impossible `!` allowlist under a directory-form ignore; a hook id that didn't exist at the pinned rev) motivated it — extend the smoke test when adding template-stamping skills.

## Skill file format

Each skill lives at `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter:

```yaml
---
name: skill-name
description: shown to Claude for auto-invocation matching
allowed-tools: Bash Read Write Edit
argument-hint: "[--flag | optional arg]"   # shown in user-facing help; optional
disable-model-invocation: true             # user-invoked only; see below
---
```

Shell commands in ` ```! ` blocks run before Claude sees the skill content — use for injecting live repo state (git status, log, diff).

**If a skill's logic depends on discovering neighbouring files, `allowed-tools` must grant `Glob`/`Grep` — the failure is silent.** Without them the skill cannot list a directory or search sibling files, so a step phrased as "look for related files before deciding" simply never runs, and the skill falls through to whatever it can infer from the single path it was handed. Nothing errors; the discovery step just evaporates. `figure-review` shipped this way: its whole panel-vs-standalone determination rests on finding sibling panels, while `allowed-tools` granted only `Bash Read Write`, which would have reduced the check to a filename guess. `Bash` alone is not a substitute — `ls`/`grep` work, but the skill body has to say to use them, and a body written in terms of "look for" will not.

### Invocation control: user-invoked vs model-invokable

`disable-model-invocation: true` is a **supported** SKILL.md frontmatter key (verified at code.claude.com/docs/en/skills). It blocks Claude from auto-invoking the skill and prevents preloading into subagents; the `/slash` command still works — but only when it leads the submission (see "Slash-command expansion is position-sensitive" below). The companion key `user-invocable: false` does the inverse (hide from the `/` menu; Claude-only background-knowledge skills).

**Non-obvious gotcha:** the field does **not** reclaim description token budget — the description stays in the model's selection context, so the model still *sees* it and may try to invoke it; only the tool-call is blocked. Don't add this field expecting token savings — add it for invocation control. The only real token lever is keeping the `description` short, and the lint enforces a cap. Version, evidence tier, and the upstream bug numbers for both facts: `docs/harness-behavior.md` rows 9 and 11 — the cap in particular is *reported*, not observed, so re-verify the exact number before relying on it.

Skills carry the field on the **user-invoked vs model-invokable** axis:
- **User-invoked** (`disable-model-invocation: true`) — orchestrators you type explicitly: `grill-me`, `handoff`, `pickup`, `slack-message`, `create-alert`, `tab-setup`, `write-new-skill`, `pathfinder`, `ai-review`, `commit-batch`, `repo-init`, `spot-ai`.
- **Model-invokable** (no field) — Claude or another skill may reach them mid-task: `figure-review`, `grilling`, `lit-review`, `overbaked`, `reviewer-2`, `unstale`, `evolve-claude-md`, `commit-batching`, `worklog`.

**A gated skill only expands at the head of a submission — and whether the `Skill` tool can reach it by name is version-dependent, so don't design around either answer.** The CLI won't expand it mid-sentence: no `<command-name>` block, no injected body, so nothing visibly happens. What happens on an explicit `Skill(<name>)` call has flip-flopped across CLI versions: at 2.1.221 it ran normally (gating seemed to govern only autonomous selection), but at 2.1.224 it hard-rejects with an explicit error naming the field and instructing the model not to replicate the workflow by other means. At current versions, then, a gated skill is reachable **only** by a user-typed leading `/slash-command` — which makes the launcher/core split load-bearing, not just an argument-capture convenience: the gated launcher is what you type, the ungated core is what another skill can reach mid-task. Expansion mechanics (argument capture, what happens with several commands in one submission), their evidence tiers, and the CLI version they were seen on live in `docs/harness-behavior.md` — that file is the register, so check it before relying on any of them and record new observations there, not here.

**Composition rule:** a user-invoked skill may invoke model-invokable skills, never another user-invoked one. (`handoff` → `evolve-claude-md` and `handoff` → `worklog` are why both are model-invokable; `grill-me` → `grilling` is the same pattern — `grill-me` is a thin launcher so the `grilling` core stays reachable mid-task; `repo-init` → `grilling` likewise.) The 4 reviewer subagents are out of scope for this field — subagents use their own description-based invocation.

**Interactive gates need the full triad.** A skill step that must *ask the user before acting* (repo-init's intake grill is the reference case) will be skipped by a low-effort executor if stated as a plain instruction — observed live: a session default of `effortLevel: low` blew straight past "ask these questions first" and scaffolded with assumed defaults. The pattern that holds: (1) a **hard gate** stated up top ("create nothing until…"), (2) an **Anti-Rationalization table** pre-empting the specific excuses ("dir is empty, nothing to ask", "I can infer defaults"), and (3) a **Verification checklist** whose first items are the gate. Additionally, user answers must be recorded **verbatim** (quoted) in the output artifact — a gate-skipping model that invents answers otherwise forges plausible-looking records; quoting makes fabrication checkable against the transcript.

Skills may include companion reference files (e.g., `REFERENCE.md`, `CC-STYLE.md`, `COLORBLIND.md`) in the same skill directory. Load them at runtime using the same `!` block syntax above, pointing at the deployed path: `cat ~/.claude/skills/<name>/COMPANION.md 2>/dev/null || echo "(not found)"`. This keeps SKILL.md lean while injecting richer context at load time. Only the deployed path (`~/.claude/skills/`) is referenced — the repo copy in `skills/` is synced there by `sync.sh push`.

### Catalog tables (generated — don't hand-edit)

The skill/agent tables above, and the ones in `README.md`, are generated by `scripts/gen-docs.sh` from a `catalog:` frontmatter block — this used to be three hand-maintained copies (CLAUDE.md, README.md, and this SKILL.md's own list of skills) that drifted twice. When adding or editing a skill, set `catalog: {order: <int>, summary: '<one-liner>'}` in its `SKILL.md` frontmatter (`order` only sorts CLAUDE.md's table and steps by 10 — 10, 20, 30… — so a new skill slots between two neighbors by taking the gap, e.g. 45, touching one file instead of renumbering the tail) (agents use `catalog: {order, domain, reviews_for, summary}` instead of a single `summary`); set `claude_md: false` to exclude a skill from CLAUDE.md's table (e.g. the external `tab-setup` skill) and `repo_url` to render it as a link in README. For third-party work, add a `provenance` block — `{relation: authored|adapted|forked, author, url}` — and leave the attribution *out* of the `summary`; `gen-docs.sh` renders the "By / Adapted from / Forked from" suffix from it, so the credit can't drift between the two tables (it did: a skill's summary once said "By" while its description said "Adapted from"). Use `authored` for a verbatim upstream skill, `adapted` when you've meaningfully changed it, `forked` for a maintained fork. Then run `bash scripts/gen-docs.sh write` and commit the result — `.github/workflows/lint.yml` runs `gen-docs.sh check` in CI and fails the build if the committed tables don't match. `pathfinder`'s own "reach for it when" tables are hand-written on purpose (different framing than a one-line summary) and aren't generated; `gen-docs.sh` doesn't check it.

**Shell lint (`scripts/lint-shell.sh`).** ShellCheck `-S warning` over every tracked `*.sh`, discovered with `git ls-files` so a new script is covered as soon as it's committed. It is the **single source of truth**: both `.github/workflows/lint.yml` and `sync.sh`'s `lint_shell` call it, because the target list used to be inlined in the workflow and had already drifted (the step was named "all tracked shell scripts" while omitting `settings/statusline-command.sh`). Two non-obvious details, both learned by shipping an SC2115 to `main`: **ShellCheck lives at `~/.local/bin/shellcheck`** (pip `shellcheck-py`) and is often *not on `PATH`*, so the script resolves that path explicitly — the local gate had been silently skipping shell checks while CI enforced them; and the missing-linter path **degrades to a warning locally but hard-fails under `REQUIRE_SHELLCHECK=1`**, which CI sets, so a linter that vanishes can never turn into a quiet pass. When adding a `rm -rf "$VAR/sub"`, write `"${VAR:?}/sub"` — SC2115 fails the build otherwise, and the guard doesn't depend on a reader tracing the enclosing control flow. **Know the gate's blind spot:** ShellCheck does *not* flag unquoted expansion in `for x in $var`, because word-splitting there is usually intended — so it also says nothing about the **pathname** expansion that comes with it. That is the whole hazard `set -f` exists to stop in `hook-warn-stacked-commands.sh`, and it is invisible at `-S warning` *and* at `-o all` (which emits only SC2250/SC2292 style nits). When a script's correctness rests on a line the linter can't see, say so in a comment at the line — for that class of bug the comment is the only guard, and a future refactor will otherwise read the line as redundant.

**Hand-maintained user docs:** `docs/harness-behavior.md` is the register for *observed* Claude Code behavior — undocumented parser/loader/settings internals, each row carrying an evidence tier (observed / inferred / reported), the CLI version it was seen on, and its confounds. Volatile harness facts go there, not here: this file is loaded on every run, and nothing in CI can test a claim about a proprietary CLI. **When promoting a consequence out of the register into this file, prefer claims that fail loudly.** The one fact promoted here previously ("a gated skill named mid-sentence has no invocation path") was also the only one nobody re-tested — precisely because it read as settled — and it was wrong for weeks until a probe aimed at something else tripped over it (register row 9b). A claim whose failure mode is silence gets no feedback from being stated confidently in an always-loaded file; it just becomes load-bearing. **This has now happened three times, and the last two were cheaply testable** — the `.ai/` tracking-leak claim (corrected 2026-08-07) needed a five-line scratch repo to falsify, and the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`-in-`env` claim needed one `grep` of the file it described. So the lesson is not only "prefer claims that fail loudly": **when a claim here is about tool behavior you can measure in a minute, measure it rather than reasoning about it** — especially when re-reading it during unrelated work, since that is how all three were caught. `docs/configuration.md` documents each skill's config surface (env vars, connectors, degradation behavior) for external users — nothing generates or lints it, so update it whenever a skill's env vars, required connectors, or no-config fallback behavior change. Same for the `skill_deps()` map in `scripts/sync.sh` when skill-to-skill wiring changes (see Syncing skills).

## Session workflow

These skills form a session lifecycle:
- **Start**: `/pickup` — loads handoff, reports state, recommends next action
- **End**: `/handoff` — writes `.ai/HANDOFF.md`, then runs `evolve-claude-md`
- **Anytime**: `/evolve-claude-md` — standalone CLAUDE.md update
- **Planning**: `/grill-me` — stress-test a design before implementing

The `.ai/` directory is repo-local and is gitignored.

**Review-report archiving:** the six review skills (`ai-review`, `figure-review`, `reviewer-2`, `overbaked`, `unstale`, `spot-ai`) archive each report to `.ai/reviews/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<skill>[-<slug>].md` by default; `--no-archive` opts out. Archiving is best-effort (never blocks the review) and warns — without editing anything — when `.ai/` isn't gitignored in the target repo. When adding a new report-producing skill, adopt the same `## Archive` block. Each archived report also carries a **YAML provenance header** (`skill`, `skill-version`, `reviewed-repo` + short SHA/dirty, `cli`, `date`) written to the archived file only, never to the report shown to the user — so a report re-read later can be placed against a revision of the skill's criteria. `skill-version` comes from a `.version` file `deploy_skill()` stamps into each **deployed** skill dir (the deployed dir is not a git checkout, so nothing else reaches that provenance at review time); it is gitignored as `skills/*/.version` because `sync.sh pull` would otherwise round-trip it back into `skills/` as a tracked file, and it is absent — hence `unknown` — under a plugin install. Any value that fails to resolve becomes `unknown` rather than being dropped, and never blocks the archive. **Gotcha (verified 2026-07-29):** probe the ignore with the **file path at repo root** — `git check-ignore -q "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.ai/reviews/…"` — never the bare `.ai` directory. `git check-ignore -q .ai` false-negatives (exits "not ignored") for the directory-form `.ai/` pattern this ecosystem uses whenever the `.ai/` dir doesn't exist yet — e.g. the first archive in a freshly `repo-init`-scaffolded repo. All six review skills plus `create-alert` now use the correct form (migrated 2026-08-07). `spot-ai` goes further and **skips archiving entirely** when `.ai/` isn't ignored or `.ai/reviews` is a symlink, because its reports can embed author-specific measured rates.

**An archived report inherits its target's sensitivity.** Reviewing a document that contains PII creates a *second* copy of that PII under `.ai/reviews/` — and the review skills quote instances in context by design, so the copy is deliberate, not incidental (`spot-ai` quotes every finding's instance; `figure-review` quotes captions). Gitignoring `.ai/` prevents *publication*, not *accumulation*: observed 2026-08-19, three archived reports had quietly collected six candidate names and a colleague's email address from two reviewed documents, none of it ever committed but all of it sitting in plain text. Two consequences. **(1)** After reviewing anything with third-party personal data, delete the archived report or accept that the directory now holds that data — nothing prunes it, and `--no-archive` is the cheap prevention at review time. **(2)** Don't trust a directory-level judgment about what `.ai/reviews/` contains: the audit that found this had to grep every file for email addresses and names, and the report that was missed on a first pass was the one nobody expected to carry PII (a two-sentence daily note). The same reasoning extends to session scratchpads, which hold the *source* text a review was run against.

**The probe and the `mkdir` must be anchored the same way.** All six review skills were authored with a cwd-relative `mkdir -p .ai/reviews` against prose that said "under the repo root"; **all six now anchor both lines** to `mkdir -p "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.ai/reviews"` (migrated 2026-08-07). Invoked from a subdirectory, the old form scattered reports into `<cwd>/.ai/reviews/` instead of collecting them at the repo root, so the archive was not one findable place.

**Correction (measured 2026-08-07):** this paragraph previously claimed a half-migration "lands the report in a **tracked** directory immediately after reporting 'yes, ignored.'" That is **false for the pattern this ecosystem actually uses.** A gitignore entry of `.ai/` is *unanchored*, so it matches a directory named `.ai` at **any depth** — a subdirectory archive is still ignored. The tracking leak appears only under an **anchored** `/.ai/` pattern, which neither this repo's `.gitignore` nor the one `repo-init` stamps (`skills/repo-init/TEMPLATES.md:30`) uses. Both forms were verified in a scratch repo. Keep the anchoring for findability and prose-code agreement; do not justify it with a tracking leak that only bites third-party repos using the anchored form. `spot-ai` is stricter than the other five by design — it **skips archiving entirely** when `.ai/` isn't ignored or `.ai/reviews` is a symlink, because its reports can carry author-specific measured rates, and a third-party repo on the anchored form is exactly where that would leak. Note also that `figure-review` is the only review skill with a **four**-verdict vocabulary (`pass` / `flag` / `by-design?` / `cant-assess`) — the others have three, so don't assume the set is shared when editing one.

**Review skills must distinguish a chosen tradeoff from a defect (learned 2026-08-04, `figure-review`).** A criterion-checklist reviewer applied to a real scientist's figures flags mostly *intentional* choices, and an author who is overruled-then-re-flagged stops trusting the tool. Four consecutive false positives against one archive drove a redesign of `figure-review`; the lessons generalize to any review skill:

- **A panel is not a figure.** Panels of a composite delegate **legend and symbol definitions** to the shared caption and sibling panels. Reviewing `Fig_3B.pdf` standalone manufactures a missing-legend finding that does not exist in the published artifact. Any skill judging self-containment must first establish **standalone vs panel** (signals: panel-style filename, a sibling differing by one letter, one notebook saving many panels) and state the assumption when it can't tell — which means it needs `Glob`/`Grep` in `allowed-tools`, or the sibling check silently never runs and the whole scheme rests on a filename guess. Two refinements learned the hard way: **`n` and data source are not reliably delegable** (a composite caption routinely covers several panels without mapping which is which, and those are the two items most often dropped), and a delegated item must be reported **`cant-assess`, never silence** — when the composite itself isn't an input, "probably covered elsewhere" is an inference, not a finding, and silent suppression is indistinguishable from a clean bill of health.
- **Publication stage sets the prior.** A published figure is post-peer-review, so apparent defects are far more likely deliberate. `figure-review` now raises them as a distinct `by-design?` verdict rather than `flag`, which lets the author confirm or overrule in one line.
- **Reproductions are out of scope.** When a figure deliberately reproduces a published one, its choices are *inherited*. Judge fidelity to the source, not the criteria — otherwise every flaw of the original is scored against the author.
- **Withdrawn findings must stay withdrawn.** Stated at `skills/figure-review/SKILL.md:39` (in the body, *above* `## Does not` — this line previously misreported it as living in that section). Re-raising an intentional choice in a later pass is the skill's primary failure mode. Note the rule is currently a prompt instruction with **session-scoped** memory: a later session re-reviewing the same figure has no record of what the author overruled. `spot-ai` sets the precedent for fixing this — `skills/spot-ai/SKILL.md:64` reads prior rulings back out of `.ai/reviews/`.
- **Variability ≠ estimation uncertainty.** The old criterion ("flag if a quantitative claim has no CI/spread/error bars") read as a checklist of decorations and fired on PDFs, histograms, and violins — where the distribution *is* the spread. It now splits the two: distribution-as-subject → `pass`; point estimate or derived scalar → estimation uncertainty required. It also checks whether the inputs to compute an interval even exist before prescribing one — a naive interval over strongly correlated samples overstates precision — and states that **significance masking does not satisfy the requirement**, since stippling is a binary test result from which no interval is recoverable (and the conventions contradict each other: stipple-where-significant vs hatch-where-models-disagree).
- **A rule derived from one figure is usually too narrow to ship.** Two were added on 2026-08-04 and dropped the same day, both from single figures seen that session: (1) an "interval rendered as composition" check (low/central/high as stacked bars) false-positived on the field-standard stacked sea-level budget (AR6 Fig. 9.27-style), where segments are *physical processes*, not quantiles; (2) a "tail probability or ratio of small numbers" escalation used the wrong discriminator — what determines whether a ratio is constrained is **effective sample size**, not the magnitude of the numbers, so it passed a nested-ensemble PR whose CI straddled 1 (96/1000 vs 40/1000 counts, but 20 parent GCMs → n_eff ≈ 20) while false-positiving on well-constrained large-ensemble ratios. Prefer the general branch (any claimed ratio needs estimation uncertainty) over a magnitude heuristic.
- **Quantify thresholds instead of asserting them.** "Scale appropriate for the data range" was unfalsifiable; it is now "≥2 orders of magnitude on a linear axis, and compute the span rather than asserting it."

The one part of the original that needed no change: criterion 5 (claim support) requires the text claim as input and marks `cant-assess` otherwise instead of guessing. **That restraint is the model** — extend it to the other criteria rather than the reverse.

**Calibrating a detector-style review skill (method that proved out, 2026-08).** Generate the calibration corpus with subagents kept *blind to the purpose* (an agent told "we're hunting X" suppresses or performs X); score any blind evaluation against a **sealed key written before judging**, with known findings pre-registered so a hit can't be read as post-hoc. Two hazards observed: tool-bearing "blind" drafting agents **self-ground** — they read the repo or filesystem and return researched text instead of pure generation — so record tool-call counts per specimen (or strip tools) and stratify; and when a skill ships a measurement script, **any definition change is a calibration epoch** — version-bind every derived artifact (reference rates, per-author profiles) to the script version and re-measure on mismatch, never compare rates across versions. The worked example, with corpora and scored reports, is under `.ai/spot-ai-corpus/` and `.ai/reviews/2026-08-1{3,4}-spot-ai-*.md`.

## Worklog → Notion journal

The `worklog` skill captures a single work-log entry to **three** targets (all best-effort — none may block the caller): a local `.ai/worklog-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl` mirror (source of truth), a redundant copy SSH-appended to `~/worklog/inbox/<date>.jsonl` on the configured server (`WORKLOG_SSH_TARGET`), and a bullet appended to the current week's page in the **Work Journal** Notion space. It is model-invokable — it fires whenever the user asks to log/note/record something, and `/handoff` calls it after writing `.ai/HANDOFF.md`. An end-of-day Claude routine summarizes the day's raw entries into narrative sections on that weekly page.

- **Configuration:** the server target (`WORKLOG_SSH_TARGET`) and the Notion Work Journal home page id (`WORKLOG_NOTION_HOME`) live in the `env` block of `~/.claude/settings.json` (machine-local, not in this public repo). The skill distinguishes **misconfiguration from transient failure**: an *unset* var is surfaced loudly as a setup error, while a *configured-but-unreachable* target (server down, Notion MCP disconnected) stays best-effort and falls back to the local mirror. The specific IDs are recorded in machine-local memory, not here.
- **Weekly pages** are sub-pages titled `Week of YYYY-MM-DD (…)` (Monday-anchored). Raw entries live under a `## 🗂️ Raw entries` heading pinned as the **last** section — the append is an `insert_content` at page-end and depends on that section staying last.
- **Why OAuth, not a Notion token:** the Climate Central workspace disables internal integration tokens, so the pipeline reuses the claude.ai **Notion OAuth MCP** (available in interactive sessions and cloud routines). This also means the summarization step must be a **Claude cloud routine** (which inherits the OAuth), not a server-side cron — a server cron can't reach Notion with OAuth *and* can't be reached from the cloud (private Tailscale network). The server hop is a redundant archive only.
- **Toggle→heading tradeoff:** raw entries use a plain heading, not a collapsible toggle — reliably appending *inside* a toggle via the API is fragile (append tools add page-level blocks; nesting needs exact-match search-replace). The nightly routine clears the section, so it stays short regardless.

## Boot hooks

| Hook | Script | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `SessionStart` | `~/.claude/skills/tab-setup/scripts/hook-startup.sh` | Auto-name and color-code each session on boot |
| `SessionStart` | inline `jq` command | Re-pin `model: opus` + `effortLevel: medium` as the default on every boot (self-heals a mid-session `/model`/`/effort` change) |

`hook-startup.sh` is part of the `tab-setup` skill (deployed from `dgilford/tab-setup`). It is fully self-contained — no dependency on this repo. It generates a session name via Haiku API when `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set, falling back to a deterministic wordlist hash otherwise; assigns a tab color; and prints `[pickup]` / `[env]` reminders to stderr. `sync.sh push` registers the hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` automatically.

**The key is optional, and the `env` block is the wrong place to put it.** The wordlist fallback is the normal, intended state — `docs/configuration.md` and `docs/tab-setup.md` both document the key as optional, and no machine here has ever set it. Anything in `settings.json`'s `env` block is exported into **every** Claude Code session, and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` **takes precedence over subscription auth** — so adding it there silently switches the machine from subscription to metered API billing, for the sake of a cosmetic session name. This is the same hazard guarded against elsewhere in this ecosystem: `window-warmup`'s workflow warns "Do NOT set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (it takes precedence and bills the API instead of the subscription)" and uses `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` from `claude setup-token`; `talim-server`'s heartbeat opens with a bare `unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. If Haiku naming is ever actually wanted, inject a narrowly-scoped key into the hook's own process only — never the global `env` block.

Tab color assignments are persisted in `~/.claude/project-colors.json` (cwd → {color, name, pid}), which is written by `hook-startup.sh` and never touched by the watcher. This drives color persistence through `/clear` (same PID) and `claude -c` (same cwd, dead PID not in use).

**Model/effort pin hook.** Interactive `/model` and `/effort` write their new value straight into `~/.claude/settings.json` ("saved as your default for new sessions") — there is *no* per-session opt-in for model/effort (only `fastModePerSessionOptIn` exists, and it covers fast mode alone). To keep a durable default without giving that up, a second `SessionStart` hook re-pins the desired default on every boot via `jq '.model="opus" | .effortLevel="medium"'` (tmp-file + `mv`, with `|| rm -f` cleanup so a failed `jq` never corrupts the file). A mid-session change still applies to the current session; the *next* boot heals it back — with a one-session-lag caveat (the session immediately after a change may briefly boot at the changed value before the hook fires; live-correction depends on the settings watcher, unverified). This hook is **added manually per machine, not deployed by `sync.sh`** — but it *survives* `push`, because `sync.sh`'s `SessionStart` merge only appends `hook-startup.sh` when absent (`any("hook-startup" in str(h) ...)`) and never rewrites the existing matcher entry, and statusLine reconciliation touches only `statusLine`. To set it up on a new machine, add a second command to the `SessionStart` matcher `""` hooks array: `jq '.model="opus" | .effortLevel="medium"' ~/.claude/settings.json > ~/.claude/settings.json.tmp 2>/dev/null && mv ~/.claude/settings.json.tmp ~/.claude/settings.json || rm -f ~/.claude/settings.json.tmp`.

**Stacked-command warning hook.** `scripts/hook-warn-stacked-commands.sh` is a `UserPromptSubmit` hook that warns when a submission begins with two or more slash commands — they all expand (`docs/harness-behavior.md` row 4), and that both bodies then run ungated is row 6, *inferred*. Warn-only and fails open; contracts and the reason `set -f` is load-bearing are in the script header. Three things worth knowing before writing any hook on this event: exit 0 stdout is **injected as context Claude reads** (so a hook that prints stray text is editing the prompt), **exit 2 erases the user's prompt** (this script never exits 2), and the event **does not fire for mid-turn submissions** (`docs/harness-behavior.md` row 12) — so any guard built on it, including this one, is bypassed by submitting while a turn is still running. Like the model/effort pin hook, registration is **manual per machine** — add to the `UserPromptSubmit` array in `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "bash ~/Projects/ai-science-toolkit/scripts/hook-warn-stacked-commands.sh" }] }
```

**Claude cannot edit hook commands in `~/.claude/settings.json` — the permission classifier blocks it,** via both Bash and the `Edit` tool (observed 2026-08-04; a hook command is code that runs on every prompt, so this is a deliberate guard, not a misconfiguration). Don't spend turns routing around it: either ask the user to paste the edit, or — usually better — **instrument the hook *script* instead.** The script is re-read on every invocation, so a script edit needs no restart and removes the "did the settings change take effect yet" confound that a `settings.json` edit introduces. Two further cautions when touching that file at all: its `env` block holds a **live API key** (`ZOTERO_API_KEY`; note it deliberately does *not* hold `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` — see the billing hazard above), so never copy it wholesale into a scratch or temp directory for "backup" — do targeted string swaps with the original recorded instead; and remember the `SessionStart` pin hook rewrites the file on every boot, so an edit must survive a `jq` round-trip.

## Syncing skills

Skills in `skills/` are the source of truth. Use `scripts/sync.sh` — do not use `cp -r` directly (it creates nested directories when the destination already exists).

```bash
bash scripts/sync.sh push             # deploy skills/ → ~/.claude/skills/; agents/ → ~/.claude/agents/; register hook-startup.sh
bash scripts/sync.sh push <name>...   # deploy only the named skills/agents (piecemeal install)
bash scripts/sync.sh pull             # pull ~/.claude/skills/ → skills/; ~/.claude/agents/ → agents/
```

**Named push** auto-detects each name as a skill (`skills/<name>/`) or agent (`agents/<name>.md`) and transitively auto-includes co-deployed runtime dependencies from the `skill_deps()` map in `scripts/sync.sh` — that map is the **single source of truth** for skill→skill wiring (this file deliberately doesn't duplicate the list; it drifted when it did). "Dependency" spans hard (the caller no-ops without it) and graceful-degrade (e.g. `repo-init` asks its intake questions inline if `grilling` is absent) — co-deploy both kinds. **Update `skill_deps()` when wiring changes** (`lint_skill_refs()` catches in-repo renames but not this map). A named push skips settings registration (hook/statusline) unless `tab-setup` is among the resolved names, and skips the external-repo refresh likewise. Exclusion interplay: an *explicitly named* skill overrides its machine-local exclusion; a *dependency-added* one still honors it.

After `pull`, review `git diff skills/ agents/` — pull brings in all globally installed skills and agents, including any not yet tracked in this repo.

**Always edit `skills/` (the repo copy), never `~/.claude/skills/` directly.** `push` overwrites the installed copy from the repo — edits to the installed copy are silently lost on the next push.

**A merge does not deploy — so after merging a branch that touched `skills/` or `agents/`, check for drift and *ask* the user whether to deploy. Never deploy on your own initiative.** `push` sits outside every git path, so a merge leaves the repo correct and the thing that actually runs stale, with nothing to announce it: the drifted skill keeps working, just at its old behavior. Observed 2026-08-04 — a merged `skills/handoff/SKILL.md` change went undeployed and the very next `/handoff` run executed the old body (it happened to lose only a `claude --version` preamble, and only because the version was already in context did the omission cost nothing). To check: `git diff <merge-base>..HEAD --stat -- skills/ agents/` names what changed, and comparing a repo `SKILL.md` against its `~/.claude/skills/<name>/` counterpart confirms live drift. Then surface the affected names and let the user choose. The reason this is a prompt and not an automatic step: deploying is a change to the user's live environment, a *full* `push` additionally rewrites settings registration and refreshes the external `tab-setup` fork (a named `push <skill>` does neither unless `tab-setup` resolves), and a deploy mid-session changes how subsequent invocations behave in a session already underway. Note there is no drift subcommand — `sync.sh orphans` reports deployed-without-repo-counterpart, not content drift — so the comparison is manual until someone adds one.

**`push` never prunes.** `deploy_skill()` is `mkdir -p` + `cp -r "$SKILLS_SRC/$1/." "$SKILLS_DEST/$1/"` — an overlay with no delete pass — and `deploy_agent()` is a plain `cp`. (That trailing-`/.` form is what avoids the nested-directory trap named above; it does not prune.) So three things survive deletion from the repo: a renamed or removed **skill** dir, a renamed or removed **agent** `.md`, and a **file deleted from inside** a skill that still deploys. All keep resolving from `~/.claude/` indefinitely. After any rename (`git mv`) or deletion (`git rm -r`), delete the deployed copy by hand — and do it **before the next `pull`**, because `pull` copies every deployed dir back into `skills/`, re-adding the old name to the repo. `bash scripts/sync.sh orphans` lists deployed skills and agents with no repo counterpart (report-only; it never deletes, and it will also list legitimately third-party skills installed outside this repo). Why this matters beyond tidiness: `resume` was renamed to `pickup` precisely because a local skill shadows Claude Code's built-in `/resume` past-session picker, and a lingering deployed `resume/` would silently reinstate that shadowing.

**Running `push` on Windows (Git Bash).** The script is Unix-authored and has four rough edges here; all four were hit on a first run, and the first two are unfixed bugs in `sync.sh` itself — delete these notes when they're fixed. (1) Most `python3` heredocs call `open()` with **no `encoding=`**, so Windows' cp1252 default raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on the non-ASCII already present in skill files. `lint_skill_refs()` now passes `encoding="utf-8"` (it had to — it reads the widest file set in the repo), but `lint_frontmatter()`, the settings-merge heredocs, and `scripts/gen-docs.sh` still don't. Prefix `PYTHONUTF8=1` until they do — worth fixing in-repo rather than per-machine, since the repo is public and plugin-distributed. (2) The `tab-setup` review gate's `read -r reply` runs under `set -euo pipefail`, so on **non-TTY stdin the EOF return aborts the script silently** — it never reaches the intended `✗ declined — rolling back` path, deploying nothing and rolling back nothing. That's what a `!`-shell or piped invocation gets; `read -r reply || reply=n` would make it degrade to "No" as designed, and `SYNC_EXTERNAL_ACCEPT=1` is the deliberate non-interactive escape hatch. (3) **Missing PyYAML degrades inconsistently** — `lint_frontmatter()` skips with a warning, but `tests/smoke_repo_init.py` hard-fails on every yaml block, so the push dies with a confusing template error instead of one clear "install PyYAML". (4) On Windows `python3` usually resolves to the **Windows Store stub**, which prints an install prompt and exits nonzero rather than failing cleanly; a `python3.exe` copy of `python.exe` in the real install dir fixes it if that dir already precedes `WindowsApps` on PATH. Note also that Git for Windows puts `bash.exe` in `Git\bin`, which the installer does **not** add to PATH (only `Git\cmd`, which has `git.exe` alone).

**Machine-local push exclusions:** to keep a skill out of `push` on **one** machine without affecting others, list its dir name (one per line, `#` comments allowed) in `~/.claude/sync-skills-exclude`. `push` skips each match (printing `⤫ <name> (excluded…)`) via `is_excluded()`. The file is machine-local and untracked, so the choice never propagates through the repo; the mechanism itself lives in `scripts/sync.sh`. This is a *deploy* gate only — nothing here deletes (see "`push` never prunes" above), and a skill can still be disabled other ways (e.g. on the deployment where `worklog` is excluded, it is also inert without its `WORKLOG_*` creds — but that exclusion is that machine's local choice, not a repo-wide fact).

**Keeping a not-yet-public skill in this public repo:** leave its directory untracked and list it in `.git/info/exclude` (machine-local — a `.gitignore` entry would itself publish the name). Two couplings make this a *fragile* state, learned building one such skill: (1) `gen-docs.sh write` regenerates the catalog tables from the filesystem, so CLAUDE.md/README acquire rows referencing the excluded skill — **those files become uncommittable** until the skill ships (a checkout without the skill fails both `gen-docs.sh check` and `lint_skill_refs` in CI), which forces go-public to be one atomic commit: skill + tables + pathfinder row + axis-list entry together, then delete the exclude line. (2) Untracked + excluded means `git clean -fdx` deletes the only repo copy — keep a backup outside the repo while the state persists.

**External skills** (`tab-setup`) are a special case: `push` pulls from `github.com/dgilford/tab-setup` (a fork of `JeraldHuff/tab-setup`) into `tab-setup/` *before* copying into `skills/tab-setup/`, so **edits to `skills/tab-setup/scripts/` and `skills/tab-setup/vscode-extension/` are overwritten by this pull** — edit `tab-setup/scripts/`, commit/push to the fork, then `sync.sh push`. **The refresh is narrower than it looks, and the difference is load-bearing:** `sync_external_skills()` copies *only* those two subdirectories (`scripts/sync.sh:185-194`) and never `SKILL.md`, which is why the local `catalog:` block that `skills/tab-setup/SKILL.md` carries — `claude_md: false`, `repo_url`, `provenance` — survives a push and `gen-docs.sh check` keeps passing. The fork's own `SKILL.md` has no `catalog:` block; if the refresh ever widened to the whole tree, every push would silently drop the tab-setup row out of README's table. The push now shows a diff and asks before deploying changed upstream code (it becomes a SessionStart hook). Fork-maintenance procedures (upstream sync, `/tab-setup update`, caveats): `docs/tab-setup-maintenance.md`.

**The claude-tab VS Code extension is deliberately duplicated** — `tab-setup/vscode-extension/` (the fork; what deploys) and the tracked `vscode-extension/` (what CI lints and unit tests, since `/tab-setup/` is gitignored and therefore invisible to CI). Both are load-bearing, so **author in the fork, then mirror into `vscode-extension/`**; `lint_vscode_extension()` in `sync.sh` fails the push on drift (skipped when `tab-setup/` is absent). They drifted undetected for weeks in both directions, which cost the whole `/color` injection path under code-server. The failure mode is silent by construction: a missing extension file still **registers** in `extensions.json`, so installers report success and `setup.sh` keeps writing `~/.claude/.pending-color` — but `activate()` throws, nothing consumes the file, and the only evidence is one `Activating extension … failed` line in the newest `~/.local/share/code-server/logs/*/exthost*/remoteexthost.log`. An unconsumed `.pending-color` is the fastest smell. Two installers had the same enumerated-copy bug (both omitted a newly added `lib/`), so **copy the extension tree wholesale, never file-by-file**. Related trap, **observed live 2026-08-07** (not merely predicted): `sync.sh` never rewrites `~/.claude/skills/tab-setup/.repo-path`, so relocating the checkout breaks `/tab-setup update` silently — and that path is the only one running `install.sh`'s verify diff, which is what surfaces files deleted upstream but lingering in the deployed dir. The pointer was found stale on this machine, still naming the pre-rename `…/ai-tools/tab-setup`, with `watcher.sh` (deleted upstream in fork `c1b3e62`) sitting undetected in the deployed dir as the downstream consequence. **The general cause is the 2026-07-17 `ai-tools`→`ai-science-toolkit` repo rename**, which is already known to break external hardcoded references — so treat any *absolute path pinned outside the repo* as suspect after a rename, and grep for the old name when one lands. Nothing lints these; the file lives in `~/.claude/`, so no repo diff will ever show it.

**Editing `extension.js` — three things that aren't visible in the file.** (1) **Never let a value from `.pending-color` reach `terminal.sendText` unvalidated.** `sendText` *submits* its argument, so a carriage return inside `color` or `name` ends the `/color`/`/rename` line early and runs the remainder as a second command. The line-based parse drops `\n`, which leaves `\r` as the reachable case — and these values are less trusted than they look: `name` defaults to `basename "$PWD"` in `setup.sh`, and Linux permits `\r` in a directory name, so opening a session inside a hostile checkout was enough (verified against the pre-guard build, which passed the injected text straight through). The guard rejects rather than sanitizes, and sits *after* the pending file is consumed so the bail can't spin. It currently has **no regression test** — don't remove it as dead defensiveness. (2) **Unit-testing this file requires stubbing `vscode`**, which only exists inside the extension host: intercept `Module._load` to return a stub, and point `HOME` at a temp dir, since `PENDING_FILE`/`SESSIONS_DIR` derive from `os.homedir()`. That's the only way to exercise `applyPending` outside VS Code. (3) **`lint_vscode_extension()` compares the tracked copy to the fork — not to what's deployed.** Deploy staleness is invisible to it (observed: four deployed `install.sh` copies a commit behind a pushed fix), and is caught only by `install.sh`'s verify diff on the `/tab-setup update` path. After changing the extension, redeploy *and* reinstall — a running extension host keeps the old build until the window reloads.

## Plugin distribution

The repo is also installable as a **Claude Code plugin** via `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` + `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` at the repo root. One-line adoption:

```
/plugin marketplace add dgilford/ai-science-toolkit
/plugin install ai-science-toolkit@ai-science-toolkit
```

- **Single bundle plugin**, `source: "."` (repo root). `plugin.json` carries metadata only — no `skills`/`agents` component fields — so Claude Code **auto-discovers** `skills/*/SKILL.md` and `agents/*.md`. This ships the same skills and agents as a full `sync.sh push` (everything, including `tab-setup`; unlike `push`, it isn't narrowed by a machine's local exclude-list and doesn't register the boot hook or refresh the tab-setup fork), so no manifest edit is needed when adding a skill or agent. Note the default `skills/` scan **always** runs and the `skills` field only *adds* to it — there is no way to exclude a skill (e.g. `tab-setup`) short of relocating it out of `skills/`.
- **`tab-setup` under the plugin path is inert, not broken:** its SessionStart auto-naming hook is registered by `sync.sh` into `~/.claude/settings.json`, not by a `hooks/hooks.json`, so a plugin install ships the `/tab-setup` command but never activates the boot hook. Users who want the hook must use `sync.sh push`.
- **`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` gotcha (companion files):** a plugin installs under `~/.claude/plugins/cache/…`, *not* `~/.claude/skills/`, so any skill that loads a companion file must **not** hardcode `~/.claude/skills/<name>/`. Use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:+$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT/skills/<name>}` with a `$HOME/.claude/skills/<name>` fallback so the same line resolves under **both** plugin install (var set → plugin root) and `sync.sh` deploy (var unset → home). **Empirically confirmed (2026-07-20):** Claude Code *does* export `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` into a skill's `` ```! `` preamble under a plugin install (not just for hooks/commands) — verified by loading `/figure-review` from a real `/plugin install` and seeing both companion files resolve — so the plugin-root branch actually fires; the pattern is not merely theoretical. `figure-review`'s `COLORBLIND.md`/`CC-STYLE.md` loads are the reference example; `create-alert`'s `HARDENING.md` (an injection-hardening block baked *verbatim* into every cloud-routine prompt it generates — the reusable pattern for any skill that authors an unattended agent holding a connector + shell) uses the same load line; `lit-review`'s relative markdown link to `REFERENCE.md` needs no such handling (resolved from the SKILL.md's own dir). Apply this rule to any new companion-file skill.
- **Versioning:** two of the repo's four `version` fields live here — the marketplace manifest's top-level `version` and `plugin.json` (the plugin entry in `marketplace.json` carries no metadata beyond `name`/`source`/`category`/`description`; everything else is inherited from `plugin.json`, the authoritative source). Bump both on a tagged release so `/plugin marketplace update` surfaces the change. The other two are `CITATION.cff` and `.zenodo.json` — see the full list under Releases & citation. Nothing lints any of them against git tags.

## Cloud routines

Warmup infrastructure (the two-tier `claude -p` window-anchoring system and its `warmup health check` routine) lives in the private infra repo, not here.

A weekly cloud routine, `disable-model-invocation bug watch` (ID in `.ai/routines.md`), polls anthropics/claude-code#22345 + the CHANGELOG and alerts when the token-reclaim bug (see Skill file format) is fixed; retire it then. **Caveat:** #22345 is titled as a *plugin*-skills issue — a weak proxy in both directions — so on any FIXED alert, verify token reclaim empirically before acting.

Manage routines at https://claude.ai/code/routines — IDs and creation notes in `.ai/routines.md` (gitignored, machine-local).

**Routine conventions & constraints** (apply to any routine authored by `create-alert` or edited via the `schedule` skill / `RemoteTrigger` API):
- **Standard alert output** follows `create-alert`'s house format: lead each Slack message with a status glyph — **🔵** the watched-for thing happened · **🟢** ran clean, nothing to report · **⚠️** couldn't run (source/auth failure) — in Slack mrkdwn (single-asterisk `*bold*`, `:emoji:`, `•`, `·`; never `**`/`#`), with fail-loud delivery (a 🔵 that fails to send is a hard error, never a silent success). The `disable-model-invocation bug watch` and the (infra-repo) `warmup health check` routines were standardized to this scheme.
- **Cloud routines have no secret store.** Per Claude Code docs, "a dedicated secrets store is not yet available" — env vars set on a cloud environment are **plaintext-readable to anyone using that environment**. Use only for a single-user private environment, with a minimally-scoped, rotatable token.
- **Never inline a secret in a routine prompt.** The `RemoteTrigger` create/update classifier **blocks any body containing an inline credential** (e.g. a `github_pat_…`), so a credentialed routine *must* reference it via an env var (e.g. `Bearer $SOME_PAT`) — this is both the security practice and a hard requirement for programmatic updates to go through.
- **Setting a routine's env vars is a UI action** (no API, no standalone settings URL): claude.ai/code → open the routine's edit form → the cloud-icon environment selector below Instructions → hover the environment → gear → **Environment variables** (`.env` format).

## Releases & citation

**Four version slots** must be bumped together, and nothing lints them against each other or against the git tag: `CITATION.cff` (plus `date-released`), `.zenodo.json`, `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`. **`.zenodo.json` is the easy one to miss** — it isn't referenced from the plugin docs and never surfaces in a `/plugin` workflow. Grep for the outgoing version across the repo before tagging.

Tagged releases are archived to Zenodo (the repo↔Zenodo webhook is enabled), which mints a DOI. Non-obvious convention for the two DOI slots — **do not swap them on future releases:**
- **`CITATION.cff` `doi:` → the version DOI** (pins the specific release; bump it each release alongside `version`/`date-released`). It must track `version:` — a concept DOI here would contradict the version number sitting next to it, and FORCE11 software-citation practice is to cite the specific version used.
- **`CITATION.cff` `identifiers:` → both DOIs**, each with a `description` (the CFF-spec pattern), so the never-stale concept DOI is still discoverable from the citation file. Update the versioned entry's value *and* its description each release.
- **`README.md` badge → the concept (all-versions) DOI** (always resolves to the latest release; leave it unchanged across releases).

**Chicken-and-egg:** Zenodo mints the version DOI *from* the published release, so the DOI naming a release can never be inside that release's own archive — it always lands one commit after the tag. Don't try to fix this by pre-tagging; just paste it in on `main` afterward.

**Look the new DOI up, never guess it** — version record ids are not sequential with the concept id (v1.0.0 was `…21461069`, one past the concept `…21461068`; v1.1.0 was `…21682976`, nowhere near). The concept record id redirects to the latest version, so one call resolves it and confirms the webhook actually fired:

```bash
curl -sL "https://zenodo.org/api/records/<CONCEPT_ID>" | python3 -c \
  "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d['doi'], d['metadata']['version'])"
```

**The stale-DOI trap is three-legged**, and the third leg rots silently: the top-level `doi:`, the versioned `identifiers` value, *and* that entry's `description` (which names the version in prose, so YAML validation can't catch it). After editing, assert the old DOI is gone rather than eyeballing it: `grep -q '<OLD_VERSION_DOI>' CITATION.cff && echo STALE`.

Zenodo only captures releases published *after* the webhook was enabled, and only a real GitHub **Release** (not a bare `git tag`) fires it. Cutting a release: publish a GitHub Release for tag `vX.Y.Z` from `main` (e.g. `gh release create vX.Y.Z --target main`, or the web UI).

## Commits

Global GPG signing is disabled (`commit.gpgsign` is unset in `~/.gitconfig`), so commits are unsigned by default and can be made in-session without a passphrase prompt. The signing key (`user.signingkey`) is still configured — opt into a signed commit per-commit with `git commit -S`. To restore signing-by-default: `git config --global commit.gpgsign true` (note: pinentry's GUI times out in this environment, so signed commits would then need an external terminal with the key already unlocked).

**`origin/HEAD` may be unset in a clone**, which breaks any skill whose preamble diffs against it — `/security-review` fails with *"ambiguous argument 'origin/HEAD...'"* rather than degrading. Fix once per clone: `git remote set-head origin --auto`. Also note those preambles use a three-dot commit range, so they see **committed** work only; to review an uncommitted working tree, diff it explicitly rather than assuming the skill picked it up.
